bib.title: Structured Output Collapses Answer Diversity Across 44 Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Structured Output Collapses Answer Diversity Across 44 Language Models", Tapan Parikh (Cornell Tech), arXiv:2607.18476v1 [cs.CL], preprint, July 2026 (20 Jul).
COVERAGE: FULL. 34,973 of 34,973 chars of the extraction (all 12 pages, including Appendices A and B and the references). Nothing skipped.

CENTRAL CLAIM: For prompts with many equally valid answers ("Name a tree."), merely asking for the reply in JSON (no schema enforcement, no constrained decoding) moves models toward the field's modal answer. The effect is stronger for tool-use-style formats (JSON, XML). It is not a decoder artifact.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. JSON request lowers field-mean answer-choice surprisal.
 number: 1.80 -> 1.58 bits (per-model delta -0.22, p=.0002)
 setup: 31 prompts x 44 models x 4 samples, requested temp 1.0, no system prompt, via OpenRouter. Surprisal is add-one-smoothed leave-one-out against the other 43 models, scored within each format column. Exact-match normalized one-word replies, no judge.
 quote: "Field-mean answer-choice surprisal falls from 1.80 bits in plain chat to 1.58 in JSON. Averaged over the 44 models the per-model ∆is −0.22 bits"
 where: p4, §4.1
2. On the unconstrained "Pick a word." prompt, the modal answer's share rises and distinct answers fall.
 number: modal share 41% -> 64% (serendipity); distinct answers 52 -> 36
 setup: same battery, JSON column, single prompt
 quote: "serendipityrises from 41% of the pool to 64% and the number of distinct words falls from 52 to 36."
 where: p4-5
3. The tax is concentrated in the most distinctive models. Only 6 of 44 are individually significant, and all six are compressions.
 number: 6 of 44 at BH-FDR q=.10. deepseek-v3.2 2.63->1.32 (-1.31); gpt-4o-mini -0.92; gpt-4-turbo -0.87; gpt-5.6-sol -0.65; qwen3 -0.45; gemini-3.1-pro -0.31. hermes-4 -0.91 just misses. Floor models barely move: claude-opus-4.8 -0.16, grok-4.5 -0.07, claude-sonnet-5 -0.05. About 38 models are indistinguishable from zero.
 setup: as claim 1; the paper declines to rank the mid-table
 quote: "exactly six of 44 models have an individually significant ∆at BH-FDRq =.10, and all six are compressions"
 where: p4, p8
4. It is a sharpener, not a re-indexer.
 number: plain-chat mode survives in 28 of 31 categories; <4% of JSON answer mass lands on words plain chat never produced. Flips: insect ant (43%) -> butterfly (60%); board game chess -> monopoly; dance salsa -> tango.
 setup: JSON vs plain, field-level modal answer
 quote: "In 28 of 31 categories the JSON modal answer is the same word as the plain-chat mode, and less than 4% of JSON answer-mass lands on words the plain census never produced."
 where: p5, §4.2
5. It is not a temperature change.
 number: self-distinctness plain 0.42, JSON 0.39, XML 0.40, YAML 0.42, CSV 0.43, brackets 0.43
 setup: distinct answers / samples, within model and category, field level
 quote: "At the field level it is nearly flat across all six columns — plain 0.42, JSON 0.39, XML 0.40, YAML 0.42, CSV 0.43, brackets 0.43 — while surprisal drops 0.22 bits under JSON."
 where: p5, §4.3
6. Not regression to the mean.
 number: split-half r=0.94; predicted shrinkage 0.05 bits vs 1.31 observed; significant compressors clear the noise null by 3.7 to 10 sigma
 quote: "split-half test-retest reliability of the census score isr=0.94, so the shrinkage a pure re-measurement predicts for the most distinctive model is0.05bits against the1.31observed"
 where: p5
7. Defaults are register-indexed. JSON erodes stable chat defaults.
 number: 144 flagged defaults (4-sample census); re-sampled at n=20, median per-sample probability 0.90; JSON significantly shifts 76 of 144 (53%) (Fisher exact per cell, BH q=.10, false-positive floor ~10%); 29% revert outright to the field mode
 quote: "significantlyshifts the answer distribution for 76 of 144 (53%) of them (Fisher exact per cell, Benjamini–Hochberg q =.10), against a false-positive floor of∼10%"
 where: p7
8. JSON also installs defaults absent from chat.
 number: 81% of JSON four-of-four answers never given in chat survive the n=20 re-sample. fable: cerulean for colour 0% -> 100% (p≈10^-11); carpenter for occupation 0% -> 90%. opus-4.8 acquires phoenix, sonnet-4.6 gold. gpt-5.6-terra and fable both answer mango 20/20 in chat; under JSON terra goes to apple 20/20, fable keeps mango 19/20.
 quote: "of the JSON answers a model gives four-of-four butneverproduces in chat, 81% survive then = 20re-sample as genuine register-only defaults"
 where: p7
9. Register gradient (compliance-conditioned field-mean delta-surprisal).
 number: JSON -0.22, XML -0.23, YAML -0.09, CSV -0.09, brackets +0.13. Compliant n: JSON 43, XML 41, YAML 37, CSV 39, brackets 43 of 44. On the 34 models compliant in all five formats: JSON -0.27, XML -0.26, brackets +0.13.
 setup: models with a wrapper compliance of at least 90% only; 5,456 calls per column
 quote: "the field-mean ∆-surprisal is −0.22 bits for JSON,−0.23for XML,−0.09for YAML,−0.09for CSV, and+0 .13for brackets."
 where: p7-8, §4.5
10. Significance of the gradient (sign-flip permutation, 20,000 draws).
 number: JSON entropy -0.20 p=.0006, per model -0.22 p=.0002; XML entropy -0.20 p=.0004, per model -0.19 p=.002. YAML p=.75 (category) and .80 (model); CSV p=.46 and .35. Brackets +0.12 p=.014 (entropy) and +0.13 p=.009 (per model). JSON vs YAML by category p<10^-4.
 quote: "JSON and XML compress on both units (entropy−0.20, p =.0006and −0.20, p =.0004; per model−0.22, p =.0002and −0.19, p =.002)."
 where: p7-8
11. Mechanism leans toward tool-use post-training, but a corpus-register component remains.
 number: Pick-a-word serendipity share: plain 41%, CSV 52%, XML 59%, JSON 64%, YAML 65%, brackets 41%
 quote: "our reading is that both are present and the post-training component dominates the battery-wide gradient."
 where: p8. The author states the black-box setup cannot separate the two.
12. Enforcement at the decoder adds almost nothing.
 number: 36-model subset: plain 1.79, request 1.56, response_format json_schema 1.53 bits (request -0.22, enforcement a further -0.03). 8 of 44 providers returned no valid output.
 quote: "is 1.56 bits under the request and 1.53 under enforcement, against 1.79 in open chat: the request does the−0.22-bit work and enforcement adds−0.03more."
 where: p9, §4.6
13. Non-compliance fakes divergence; "stranding" is not divergence.
 number: granite and mythomax emit a valid CSV wrapper ~1% of the time; granite shows a spurious +1.49 bits in CSV before conditioning. llama-4-maverick +0.56 in JSON, 100% JSON-compliant, self-JSD 0.20 vs field 0.27, 7 of 31 modal answers change. Of the 44 models, 31 become more generic under JSON and 13 rise (Fig 1 caption).
 quote: "graniteshows a spurious+1.49bits in CSV before conditioning."
 where: p8
14. Parse hygiene.
 number: 27,280 format cells; 91 (0.3%) unrecoverable nulls (YAML 56, JSON 1); parse-plus-junk survival at least 99% per model per column
 quote: "Of the 27,280 format cells, 91 (0.3%) are unrecoverable nulls, concentrated in YAML (56) and negligible in JSON (1)"
 where: p4, §3.3
15. Practical scope (the author's discussion, not tested).
 quote: "This bites where the task admits many acceptable answers — surveys, recommendations, brainstorming, judgement, tool choice — not where structured output carries a single correct value (extraction, classification, routing), for which reduced diversity is no cost."
 where: p10, §6

METHOD DETAILS
- Clauses appended verbatim, replacing "Reply with one word only.":
 json: Reply with JSON only, in the form {"word": "<your answer>"}.
 xml: Reply with XML only, in the form <word>your answer</word>.
 yaml: Reply with YAML only, in the form `word: <your answer>`.
 csv: Reply with CSV only: a header row `word`, then one data row with your answer.
 brackets: Reply with your answer inside square brackets only, like [answer].
- Prompts: 30 "Name a[n] X." plus "Pick a word." Each is a fresh single-turn conversation, with no system prompt.
- Parsing: a per-format regex strips the wrapper. Unmatched replies fall back to the census rule on the raw text. The normalizer lowercases, strips punctuation and emoji, and keeps the final alphabetic word. The junk guard drops replies over 15 words, acknowledgements, single letters and template artifacts. An echo guard drops replies whose token is the category noun or placeholder; it trims the brackets loosening from +0.16 to +0.13.

LIMITS (the author's and mine)
- Single snapshot via one channel (OpenRouter). Requested temp 1.0 is not honored uniformly across providers.
- Surprisal is panel-relative, so absolute bits are not portable across panels.
- One clause wording per format, with no paraphrase control. The author argues the gradient rules out key-priming, fill-in framing and clause length.
- Tool-call framing and other structured-output pathways were not measured. Enforcement was heterogeneous (native decoder constraint vs gateway coercion) and was read only as a battery-wide mean.
- The paper says nothing about accuracy or reasoning tasks, because the prompts have no correct answer.
- The scope is single-word answers to category prompts. It does not cover longer fields or schemas with several keys.
- Only a point estimate of each per-model delta is shown, with no per-model CIs in the text. The mid-table is declared uninterpretable. Four samples per cell; the n=20 re-sample covers only the flagged default cells.
- The brackets reversal has no settled mechanism ("we can only speculate").
- The mechanism attribution (post-training vs corpus) is inferential, since the study is black-box.
- Models are named for mid-2026 (e.g. claude-opus-4.8, gpt-5.6), so the panel will date. The author co-wrote with Claude Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and both are subjects of the study (a disclosed note).

BUILDS ON
- Parikh 2026, One-Word Census [7] (arXiv:2607.12796): the instrument, frozen and unchanged.
- Tam et al. 2024 [10] (EMNLP Industry, "Let me speak freely?") and Kurt 2024 [3] (the dottxt rebuttal): the debate on format restrictions and accuracy. The paper calls its own question orthogonal.
- Constraint and format tax: Lee et al. 2026 "The format tax" [4]; Li et al. 2026 [5]; Ray 2026 [8].
- Luan et al. 2025 [6]: automata-based steering for diverse structured generation.
- Sclar et al. 2024 [9]: sensitivity to prompt formatting.
- Mode-collapse literature: Jiang et al. 2025 (Artificial Hivemind) [1]; Kirk et al. 2024 [2]; Zhang et al. 2025 (NoveltyBench) [11].

CODE: No code snippets in the paper. The repo is named: studies/structured/ in the modelun repository (github.com/tap2k/modelun), with run_formats.py, analyze.py, probe_significance.py, analyze_rtm_splithalf.py, analyze_register_invariance.py, analyze_brackets_robustness.py and probes/format_register.json.

FIGURES: Only one figure.
- Figure 1 (p6): answer-choice surprisal for all 44 models, open chat (gray dot) vs JSON (colored dot), sorted by chat score. Blue = more generic under JSON (31 of 44); amber = score rises (13, mostly register-invariant models stranded by the collapsing field). It shows the shape of the effect: a distinctive tail sliding to an immobile floor, with the range nearly unchanged (2.2 -> 2.0). Candidate for the note.
- The extraction showed no tables. Numbers are in the text only.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean, with no garbling beyond a few missing spaces ("isprogressive"). The first lines of the cached /tmp text are page-count noise ("12 pages"), which is harmless. No embedded instructions found. Quotes were copied from the cached /tmp extraction, whose missing spaces I kept verbatim.
